crise_abri.titre: Nuclear or chemical accident: sheltering in place
crise_abri.intro: In a toxic or radioactive cloud, the safest thing is almost always to stay inside a closed building. The authorities tell you what to do through alerts, radio and TV.
etapes: Go into the nearest building and stay there.
Close doors and windows, switch off ventilation and air conditioning.
Listen to the radio or the alert messages, and follow the instructions exactly.
Don't go and fetch the children from school: the school will shelter them.
Avoid making calls to leave the network free for the emergency services: send your loved ones an SMS instead.

Iodine tablets: only when the authorities ask. They only protect the thyroid against radioactive iodine, mainly in children, young people and pregnant or breastfeeding women. In Belgium, they're available from pharmacies (information on risquenucleaire.be).
attention: Don't go out “to have a look”: stay sheltered until the authorities announce the end of the alert.
crise_abri.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of the European Commission (72 h self-sufficiency, 2026), the Belgian Crisis Centre and civil protection services. In a crisis, the authorities' instructions take precedence over this sheet.

crise_evacuer.intro: If the authorities ask you to evacuate, every minute counts. Having your bag ready and a meeting point makes all the difference.
etapes: Take your evacuation bag, your medicines, your papers and your pets.
If you're asked to and it's safe: turn off the gas, water and electricity, and lock the house.
Follow the route given by the authorities, even if it seems longer.
Tell your loved ones where you're going, and register at the reception centre if you're sent there.
If the household is separated, go to the meeting point set in your family plan.
attention: Don't go back for belongings until access is allowed.
crise_evacuer.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of the European Commission (72 h self-sufficiency, 2026), the Belgian Crisis Centre and civil protection services. In a crisis, the authorities' instructions take precedence over this sheet.

crise_sansreseau.titre: No network and no card payments
crise_sansreseau.intro: A power cut or a cyberattack can cut phone, internet and payments all at once. What's on paper and in your pocket becomes precious.
etapes: Keep cash in small notes and coins.
Keep on paper: important numbers, your family plan and the address of the meeting point.
Listen to the battery radio: it's the channel planned for when everything else fails.
SMS often get through when calls don't. Keep messages short.
112 keeps priority on the networks: in an emergency, try anyway, even without credit or a SIM card.
Bivaska works without a network: saved map, sheets, SOS, your plan and your stock.
attention: Recharge your power banks and your phone as soon as the power comes back, in case of another cut.
crise_sansreseau.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of the European Commission (72 h self-sufficiency, 2026), the Belgian Crisis Centre and civil protection services. In a crisis, the authorities' instructions take precedence over this sheet.

crise_eau_logement.titre: The hidden water in your home
crise_eau_logement.intro: If tap water is cut off or declared unsafe, your home often holds dozens of litres of usable water. You just need to know where, and which to avoid.
etapes: Hot water tank (often 100 to 200 litres): first turn off its electricity or gas, close the cold water inlet, open a hot tap in the house to let air in, then drain from the bottom tap into a clean container. Let it cool: risk of scalding.
Pipes: close the main stopcock, open the highest tap in the house, then collect the water at the lowest tap.
Toilet cistern (not the bowl), if there's no tablet or product in it: make it safe before drinking it.
Freezer ice cubes, liquid from tinned vegetables and fruit: drinkable.
Make safe any water you're not sure about: boil for at least one minute, or disinfect (see “Making water safe to drink”).
Don't ration water: drink what you need today and look for more tomorrow. Keep pool or bath water for hygiene and the toilet.
attention: Never water from radiators or central heating: it contains chemicals (antifreeze, anti-corrosion).
Don't switch an empty hot water tank back on: the element burns out. Refill it before restoring the power.
Pool, waterbed or aquarium water: never to be drunk, even filtered.
crise_eau_logement.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_couper.titre: Turning off gas, water and electricity
crise_couper.intro: In a flood, an evacuation, an earthquake or if you smell gas, knowing how to shut off the home's supplies prevents fires, electrocution and damage. Find them now, not on the day.
etapes: Electricity: switch off the main switch on the fuse box (often near the meter). Feet dry, never if water is touching the fuse box.
Water: close the main stopcock, usually near the water meter, in the cellar, garage or under the sink.
Gas: close the valve at the meter, often a quarter turn. Handle perpendicular to the pipe = closed.
Once the gas is off, don't turn it back on yourself: call the network operator or a professional, who will check the installation.
Walk round once with the whole household, put a label on each valve and note where they are in your family plan (Ready 72 h > Plan).
attention: Only turn off the gas if there's a leak, an instruction from the authorities or an evacuation: putting it back into service requires a professional.
alerte: Smell of gas: don't switch anything on or off (no lamp, switch or doorbell), don't use your phone indoors, open the windows, get out, and call the gas operator's number or 112 from outside.
crise_couper.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_calfeutrer.intro: In a toxic cloud, fire smoke or radioactive fallout, the authorities may ask you to stay indoors. A well-sealed room greatly reduces what you breathe.
etapes: Choose an inside room with as few windows as possible, big enough for the whole household.
Chemical: prefer an upper floor, as many toxic gases are heavier than air. Radioactivity: prefer the centre of the building or the cellar.
Close doors and windows, switch off ventilation, air conditioning, the cooker hood and warm-air heating.
Tape around windows and doors, and put plastic over air vents. Slip a damp cloth under the door.
Take with you: water, battery radio, torch, phone and charger, medicines, something to sit on.
Listen to the radio and wait for the authorities to announce the end of the alert before opening up and airing the room.
attention: A sealed room is only meant for a few hours: follow the authorities' instructions on duration.
Don't use a candle, stove or combustion heater in a closed room.
crise_calfeutrer.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_troc.intro: If payments and shops stop for several days, what you have and what you can do become your currency. Rationing too hard and drawing attention are the two mistakes to avoid.
etapes: Never ration water. For food, a healthy adult can last a long time on about half their usual ration, if they drink enough.
Children, pregnant or breastfeeding women, the sick and the elderly keep their full ration.
Eat first what goes off: fridge, then freezer, then reserves.

What trades well: water and purification tablets, batteries, lighters and matches, common medicines and plasters, coffee, sugar, salt, soap, toilet paper, tools and skills (repairing, treating, cooking).
Your skills are often worth more than your things: offer a service rather than showing your stock.
Discretion: don't talk about your reserves on social media, don't show everything you have, keep lighting discreet at night.
Mutual help: organise with a few trusted neighbours (childcare, shared cooking, taking turns to get news).
attention: Prescription medicines aren't for trading: a treatment taken without medical advice can be dangerous.
Tell the authorities about isolated or dependent people you know.
crise_troc.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_radio.titre: Radio: staying informed and communicating without a network
crise_radio.intro: When the internet and mobile network go down, radio remains the channel the authorities plan to use to inform people. Walkie-talkies let you stay in touch over a few kilometres.
etapes: Stay informed: listen to your country's public radio on a battery or wind-up radio (Belgium: RTBF, VRT; France: franceinfo and local stations; Luxembourg, Netherlands, Switzerland: the national public radio; UK: BBC local radio). Find their FM frequencies at home today.

PMR446 walkie-talkies: 16 licence-free channels in Europe (446.00625 to 446.19375 MHz), 0.5 W. Real range: a few hundred metres in town, 1 to 3 km in open country, much more from one hilltop to another.
Agree in advance on a channel and a sub-code within the household and neighbourhood, and on listening times (for example 5 minutes on the hour) to save batteries.
CB (27 MHz, licence-free): channel 9 is often used as an emergency calling channel and 19 by truckers, with no guarantee that anyone is listening.
Keep it short: who you are, where you are, what you need. Repeat important information twice.
Calculate the maximum range between two points with the “Radio range” tool (Learn > Field tools).
attention: No PMR or CB channel is monitored by the emergency services: in an emergency, always try 112 first.
Marine VHF (channel 16, 156.800 MHz) is reserved for boats and requires a licence, except for a genuine distress call.
Most long-wave stations (RTBF, France Inter) no longer broadcast: use FM or digital radio (DAB+).
crise_radio.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_nord_soleil.titre: Finding north with the sun and the time
crise_nord_soleil.intro: Without a compass or GPS, the sun gives north to within a few degrees, provided you know the time. Bivaska's “Find north” tool does the calculation for you, even without a network.
etapes: Open Learn > Field tools > Find north: Bivaska calculates where the sun is now, for your region and the phone's time.
Face the sun: the tool tells you how far to turn to face north.

Without a phone, in Belgium and France: the sun is due south between 12:30 and 1:30 pm in winter, between 1:30 and 2:30 pm in summer (later the further west you are). At that moment, your shadow points north.
The sun only rises due east and sets due west at the equinoxes: in winter it rises in the south-east; in summer, in the north-east.
Check with a second method when you can: stick and shadow, the North Star at night.
attention: Never look straight at the sun, even briefly.
crise_nord_soleil.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

ps_rcp.intro: A person who doesn't respond and isn't breathing normally is in cardiac arrest. Each minute without compressions cuts the chance of survival by about 10%: don't wait to be sure, start.
etapes: Check there's no danger to you. Gently shake the shoulders and speak loudly: do they respond?
If they don't respond: gently tilt the head back, lift the chin, and look for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Rare, noisy breaths (gasps) don't count.
Not breathing normally: call 112 (speaker on), ask someone to fetch a defibrillator (AED).
Hands one on top of the other in the centre of the chest, arms straight: push down 5 to 6 cm, at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute, letting the chest come back up.
If you're trained: 30 compressions then 2 rescue breaths. Otherwise, compressions only, without stopping.
As soon as a defibrillator arrives, switch it on and follow its voice. Keep going until the emergency services take over, the person wakes up, or you're exhausted.
attention: A few hours' training (Red Cross, civil protection) changes everything: in the field, you don't learn these skills from an app.
isole: Alone, with no help reachable: CPR alone rarely saves without a defibrillator. Keep going anyway as long as you can, swapping with another person every 2 minutes if there are several of you.
If the person starts breathing normally again: recovery position and constant monitoring.
ps_rcp.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_stock_long.titre: A stock that lasts for years
crise_stock_long.intro: Some dry foods keep for years, sometimes decades, if they stay cool, dry, out of the light and well sealed. They're the basis of a reserve you don't have to keep renewing.
etapes: Keep almost indefinitely, well sealed and dry: salt, white sugar, honey (it can crystallise: that's normal, warm it gently), white vinegar and cider vinegar.
Up to 30 years, but only in long-term packaging (bucket or sealed pouch with an oxygen absorber): white rice, oat flakes, whole wheat and maize grains.

Several years, well sealed: dry pasta, lentils, dried beans and peas (the older they get, the longer they take to cook), cornflour, bicarbonate of soda, instant coffee, skimmed milk powder (quality drops over time), dried vegetables.
Shorter: oils and fats (they go rancid: renew them every 1 to 2 years), whole spices (2 to 4 years to keep their flavour), brown rice and wholemeal flour (a few months: their fat goes rancid).
The four rules: cool, dry, dark, well sealed. An opened packet or ordinary shop packaging lasts much less than the durations above.
Write the purchase date on each packet, put the oldest at the front and eat them first: the reserve renews itself. Dates are tracked in Ready 72 h > Stock.
attention: No honey for a baby under one year old (risk of infant botulism).
Throw away anything that smells rancid, has taken on moisture, is mouldy or has insects in it.
Also plan water and a way to cook: rice, pasta and pulses need a lot.
crise_stock_long.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of the USDA (United States Department of Agriculture) and Utah State University Extension on long-term food storage.

crise_lampe_huile.intro: During a power cut, a jar, a cotton wick and cooking oil give a steady light for several hours. Vegetable oil burns poorly without a wick: it doesn't ignite easily, which makes this lamp safer than an improvised paraffin lamp.
etapes: Take a thick glass jar (preserving jar type) with a metal lid.
Drill a 6 to 10 mm hole in the centre of the lid. Ideally, fix a wick holder or a large washer on it to hold the wick upright.
Use a pure cotton wick (cotton cord or string, never synthetic: synthetics melt). Thread it through the hole; it must reach the bottom.
Fill the jar two-thirds with cooking oil (sunflower, rapeseed, olive…), screw on the lid.
Let the wick soak for a few minutes, then light it. It should stick out about 1 cm: longer and the flame smokes; shorter and it goes out.
A thin wick lasts longer, a thick wick gives more light. Trim the charred tip now and then.
attention: Never leave it burning unattended, or while you sleep.
Put it on a stable, heat-resistant surface, away from curtains, fabric and children.
Ventilate the room: any flame uses oxygen and produces a little soot.
To put it out, smother the flame with a lid. Never pour water on burning oil.
The lid and the top of the jar get hot: let them cool before touching or refilling.
crise_lampe_huile.source: Written for Bivaska based on the recommendations of civil protection and crisis services (EU, Belgium, France, FEMA). In a crisis, follow the authorities' instructions.

crise_toilettes.titre: Toilets and hygiene without running water
crise_toilettes.intro: When water or sewers stop working, dirty hands and badly managed excrement make you ill faster than hunger. A few simple rules prevent diarrhoea and infections.
etapes: Dry toilet: a bucket with a lid (or the toilet bowl emptied of water), a strong bin bag inside, and a material to cover after each use: sawdust, cold wood ash, cat litter, dry soil.
Two-bucket method if possible: one for urine (much less dirty, it can be diluted and poured on uncultivated ground, away from wells), one for faeces. Separating them greatly reduces smells.
Close the bag when it's a third full, double it, and store it outside in a closed bin, in the shade, until collections resume.
If the sewers overflow or the authorities ask, stop flushing: dirty water could come back up into your home or your neighbours'.

Hands: wash them after the toilet and before eating or cooking, even with very little water. A container with a tap or a pierced bottle over a basin, a little soap: 20 seconds of rubbing. Hand gel helps if hands aren't visibly dirty.
Body wash: a flannel and a basin of lukewarm water are enough; start with the face, finish with the feet and intimate areas. Change underwear as often as possible.
Periods: keep a reserve of disposable products for several cycles. A menstrual cup or washable pads mean you won't run out; wash them in cold then boiling water if possible.
Washing-up: scrape first, then wash in a basin of hot soapy water and rinse in disinfected or boiled water. Let it air-dry.
attention: Diarrhoea in several members of the household: step up handwashing even more and give the sick person their own toilet if possible.
Never dump human waste into a stream or near a well.
crise_toilettes.source: Written for Bivaska based on official recommendations (WHO, Red Cross, civil protection, USDA, CDC). If in doubt about someone's health, call 112.
